newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel sets ultimatum to SPD to resume tax talks.
newsitem.headline: Waigel sets ultimatum to SPD to resume tax talks.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel has issued an ultimatum to Germany's opposition Social Democrats: rejoin cross-party talks on tax reforms or I will legislate without you.
"If the SPD lets the talks collapse completely, we will introduce the necessary legislation," Waigel told Bild am Sonntag in an interview released on Saturday ahead of the paper's Sunday edition.
On Friday the SPD pulled out of a third round of talks on Waigel's 30 billion mark ($17.5 billion) package of tax cuts, infuriated by government plans to slash coal industry subsidies.

Waigel added that if the SPD used its majority in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament to block the legislation, "it alone will bear the responsibility for this crash course and all its consequences."

Cutting corporate and income taxes and scrapping a morass of tax breaks are the main thrust of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's bid to beat record post-war unemployment and get Germany into shape for European monetary union (EMU).

The worsening of Germany's jobs crisis this year has been enough to shake the coalition and the SPD out of a stand-off on taxes and seek a compromise which would bypass parliamentary haggling which could run into the 1998 election campaign.

But the fragile negotiating atmosphere was shattered on Friday when Bonn announced plans to slash annual subsidies to Germany's loss-making coal mines in the Ruhr and Saarland from eight billion marks now to 3.8 million marks by 2005.
The SPD said that would put 50,000 miners on the dole and lead to the loss of a further 70,000 jobs in mining regions.
Waigel said he wanted the SPD to say at its next leadership meeting on Monday when it would return to the negotiating table.
SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine, speaking at an emergency conference on the future of the coal industry in Duesseldorf on Saturday, left a new date open.
"I can't say whether the talks will start again soon," he said. "Negotiations make no sense when the coalition will not budge and there are differences of opinion within it."

The SPD rules in Germany's two coal mining states -- North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW) and Saarland. Its chief tax expert, NRW finance minister Heinz Schleusser, told the Spiegel weekly news magazine he did not want to rejoin the talks.
"The government has never slammed the door in my face like this before," Schleusser was quoted as saying.
Hermann Otto Solms, tax negotiator for coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said he was very disappointed the SPD had pulled out of Saturday's tax meeting.
He told German radio that coal subsidies and taxes were not related, adding: "No country can afford subsidies of over 100,000 marks a year for a single job."
Pit workers on Friday shut down all of Germany's 18 coal mines in protest, and, led by over 100 motorbike outriders, 5,000 demonstrated again on Saturday in Duesseldorf.
Lafontaine won loud applause from the miners when he told them: "We will not negotiate with the other side over tax cuts for top earners when at the same time miners' jobs are being put into doubt."

And, in a "Duesseldorf declaration", politicians, trade unionists, churches and other groups attending the conference said they were "stunned by the government's announcement of its plans to subsidise the coal industry".

The breakdown of negotiations to try and fix the German tax system could not have come at a worse time for Kohl, as doubts mount over Germany's ability to make the grade for the European single currency -- his pet project.

Herbert Hax, head of the "five wise men" economic advisory panel, urged a delay to EMU's planned start in 1999, saying Germany would miss the Maastricht treaty's targets both for the budget deficit and public debt.
"If you take the stability criteria seriously, Germany will probably not be able to introduce the euro as planned in 1999," he told Bild am Sonntag.
